vector.def: An ordered list of numbers, written as a column. A vector of \(p\) real numbers lives in \(\mathbb{R}^p\).

linear-combination.def: A sum of scaled vectors, such as \(3\mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}\).

dot-product.def: \(\mathbf{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}=\sum_d a_db_d\): multiply matching entries and add. Equals \(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta\).

orthogonal.def: At right angles: two vectors whose dot product is zero.

matrix.def: A rectangular table of numbers with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns (\(m\times n\)).

column-space.def: All vectors \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) can produce: every linear combination of the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\).

linear-map.def: A function \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\): keeps lines straight and the origin fixed. The columns of A are where the basic arrows land.

identity-matrix.def: \(\mathbf{I}\): ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. \(\mathbf{I}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}\).

determinant.def: For a 2×2 matrix, \(ad-bc\): the factor by which the matrix scales areas. Zero means singular (no inverse).

inverse.def: \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}\). Exists only for square matrices with non-zero determinant.

linear-independence.def: Vectors none of which is a linear combination of the others: each adds a new direction.

rank.def: The number of linearly independent columns of a matrix.

design-matrix.def: \(\mathbf{X}\): one row per observation, a column of ones then one column per predictor. Predictions are \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\).

normal-equations.def: \(\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y}\): their solution is the least-squares fit.

projection.def: The closest point to \(\mathbf{y}\) on a line or plane; the leftover is orthogonal to it. Onto \(\mathbf{u}\): \(\frac{\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}\).

eigenvector.def: A non-zero \(\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\): a direction the matrix only stretches; \(\lambda\) is the eigenvalue.
